title: Cambodia Declares Permanent Neutrality Policy
reason: Independent corroboration confirms Cambodia formalized a policy of permanent neutrality in 1957 under Sihanouk. The U.S. State Department's official Foreign Relations of the United States (FRUS) archive cites 'The Cambodian Neutrality Law of November 6, 1957' and states Cambodia 'has by now become irrevocably committed to the policy of neutrality and has formalized it in Cambodian law,' identifying this as one of Sihanouk's signature personal achievements. Independently, the French encyclopedia Universalis states 'Le 11 septembre 1957, Sihanouk faisait voter une loi proclamant la neutralité' (On September 11, 1957, Sihanouk had a law passed proclaiming neutrality) — i.e., the National Assembly vote preceded the royal Kram/promulgation, consistent with the FRUS date. Sihanouk's rejection of military alliances, specifically SEATO, is well documented (a widely-cited Sihanouk quote: 'I considered SEATO an aggressive military alliance...'; CIA/Dulles pressure to join SEATO in Jan 1956 which he refused), and neutrality became the enduring foundation of Cambodian foreign policy through the Sangkum era. One minor imprecision: the description's phrase 'enshrined in the constitution' is a simplification — the 1957 act was a National Assembly law/royal Kram, not literally a constitutional amendment (explicit constitutional Article 53 language came later, in the 1993 constitution, though French-language sources describe the 1993 provision as directly inherited from the 1957 law). This is not material enough to change country/year/core-actor/core-action, so verdict is TRUE rather than PARTIAL.

title: Samlaut Peasant Uprising Signals Growing Rural Discontent
reason: The Samlaut Uprising is a well-documented historical event: a peasant rebellion broke out on 2 April 1967 near Samlaut, Battambang Province, Cambodia, triggered by the government's forced/low-price rice-collection system ('ramassage du paddy') enforced by troops — angry peasants attacked and killed soldiers collecting rice. The Royal Cambodian government (under Sihanouk/Lon Nol) responded with violent military suppression (army sweeps, air force strafing/bombing of villages), with a death toll reported in the hundreds and thousands of villagers fleeing into the forest. It is widely regarded by historians (notably Ben Kiernan, who devoted a two-volume scholarly monograph, 'The Samlaut Rebellion and Its Aftermath, 1967-70: The Origins of Cambodia's Liberation Movement,' Monash Univ., 1975, to this exact event) as a foundational mobilization of rural discontent that fed directly into the Khmer Rouge's formal launch of armed struggle later in 1967-68. Independent (non-Wikipedia) corroboration was found on khmerization.blogspot.com, which confirms the Samlaut location, the land/rice-related grievances against provincial officials, and the rebellion's role in escalating into the civil war that the Khmer Rouge exploited. Multiple other independent leads (Kiernan's monograph listings on Google Books/HathiTrust/Semantic Scholar/Amazon/Goodreads, a ResearchGate peer-reviewed paper on Khmer Rouge state formation in NW Cambodia) all corroborate the same year, location, cause, and historical significance, though those specific pages did not load full text via WebFetch. All material details in the event description (location, trigger, suppression, death toll, and downstream link to Khmer Rouge mobilization) match.

reason: Independent sources (Wikipedia: Sa Kaeo Refugee Camp, Khao-I-Dang, Cambodian humanitarian crisis) confirm that following Vietnam's Dec 1978 invasion of Cambodia, hundreds of thousands of Cambodians fled toward the Thai border. title: PRK Begins Economic Liberalization Under Vietnamese Guidance
reason: The general phenomenon (PRK gradually easing collectivization toward limited private trade, under Vietnamese advisory influence) is real, but it is not correctly dated to 1984 and not correctly attributed to "the PRK government under Hun Sen." In 1984, Hun Sen was Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister — NOT the head of government; PM Chan Sy held that post until his death in December 1984, and Hun Sen only became Prime Minister in January 1985. Multiple sources place the actual liberalization inflection points later: the KPRP's Fifth Congress (October 1985) was where party leaders urged official recognition of the private sector, and a constitutional amendment formally legitimizing the private economy passed in February 1986. One source further notes that as of 1986, 97% of the rural population was still in the collective (Krom Samaki) sector, and Krom Samaki was only formally replaced by private land ownership in 1989 — indicating collectivization remained dominant well past 1984. The severe agricultural/food crisis that drove PRK's pragmatic policy also dates mainly to 1979-1980 (immediate post-Khmer Rouge famine), not 1984. No source found ties a specific 1984 policy initiation to Hun Sen. The described event is best understood as a mistimed/misattributed compression of a gradual 1980-1986 process, with the closest defensible "start" marker (both for the reform push and for Hun Sen's ascension to government leadership) being 1985.

On 23 Feb 2015, Cambodia deported Gonzalez-Davidson; the very next day (24 Feb 2015) PM Hun Sen announced the $400M, 108MW Cheay Areng hydropower dam (planned by China's Sinohydro Resources in Koh Kong's Cardamom Mountains/Central Cardamom Protected Forest) would be postponed, stating 'From now until 2018, there will be no permission to build [the dam].'
